::: {.oneline}
The charges set in motion by the incident light radiate light of their own, and
what leaves the sample is the sum of this radiation and the original beam.
:::

## Short answer

Nothing absorbs light by swallowing it. The incident field shakes the charges in
the material, accelerating charges radiate, and the radiated field adds to the
incident one everywhere in space. Everything we call reflection, refraction,
transmission or absorption is the outcome of this single sum.

Behind the sample the radiated field is largely out of phase with the incident
one, so that the two partly cancel. This is a reduction in transmission, which
we call absorption. In front of the sample the radiation adds up in a different
direction and becomes the reflected beam, while inside the material the same
interference slows the apparent progress of the wave, which is refraction. One
mechanism thus carries three names.

This is why a susceptibility is not yet an observable. It tells us how strongly
the charges respond, but turning this into a measured intensity requires solving
Maxwell's equations with those charges as the source, subject to the boundaries
where the sample begins and ends. Geometry enters here and never leaves, since a
monolayer, the same monolayer on a substrate, and a thick crystal of the same
material give different spectra with identical response functions.

There is a further subtlety in a real solid. The field felt by a given atom is
not the applied field, but the applied field together with everything the
neighbouring charges are radiating. In strongly inhomogeneous materials this
feedback noticeably reshapes the spectrum.

## Why it works this way

The separation into material response and field propagation is a choice made for
convenience, since the microscopic problem is one coupled system of charges and
field. Splitting it allows the response to be computed once and reused for any
geometry, which is a considerable practical advantage, at the price of
remembering that comparison with experiment is not complete until the second
half has been done.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The algebra: from susceptibility to Fresnel coefficients

For a bulk isotropic medium, $\varepsilon(\omega) = 1 + \chi(\omega)$ and
$n(\omega) = \sqrt{\varepsilon(\omega)}$, with normal-incidence coefficients

$$
r = \frac{1-n}{1+n} ,
\qquad
t = \frac{2}{1+n} ,
\qquad
\alpha(\omega) = \frac{2\omega}{c}\operatorname{Im} n(\omega) .
$$ {#eq-fresnel}

For a two-dimensional sheet of conductivity $\sigma(\omega)$ between media of
index $n_1$ and $n_2$, the boundary condition changes and the absorbance becomes

$$
A(\omega) = \frac{4\,\operatorname{Re}\sigma(\omega)/\varepsilon_0 c}
{|n_1 + n_2 + \sigma(\omega)/\varepsilon_0 c|^{2}} ,
$$ {#eq-sheet-absorbance}

which is why a supported monolayer and a freestanding one are not directly
comparable.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The algebra: local field effects

Working in reciprocal space, the macroscopic dielectric function is obtained by
inverting the full microscopic matrix and taking one element,

$$
\varepsilon_M(\omega) =
\frac{1}{\left[\varepsilon^{-1}_{\mathbf G \mathbf G'}(\omega)\right]_{\mathbf 0 \mathbf 0}} ,
$$ {#eq-macroscopic-epsilon}

which is not the same as taking the head of $\varepsilon$ directly. The
difference is exactly the local field effect, and it is large in layered and
porous systems.
:::

## Common confusions

- **"Absorption means photons are destroyed inside the sample."** The measured
  reduction is interference between the incident and the radiated fields, and
  where the energy ends up is a separate question.
- **"The dielectric function is the head of the microscopic matrix."** Only when
  local field effects are negligible.
